tagline.text: A humble sulfur hot spring at the foot of Mount Malindig in Marinduque

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱100–500 (per person, day trip from Boac, round trip including entrance fee and transport)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Marinduque Airport (MRQ, no scheduled commercial flights)

children.text: A natural sulfur hot spring at the foot of Mount Malindig in Buenavista, southern Marinduque. The entrance fee is only a few dozen pesos, so it is an easy add-on, and it is a good place to soothe tired muscles after a Malindig climb. Facilities are basic, so set your expectations accordingly.

Malbog Sulfur Spring is a natural hot spring in Barangay Malbog, Buenavista, in the south of Marinduque. It sits at the foot of Mt. Malindig, the island's highest mountain, and the warm sulfur water that flows down from the mountain collects in swimming-pool style basins. It is less a glamorous resort than a neighborhood hot spring that local people have used for a long time.

The water is a bluish white and smells like rotten eggs. Locally it has long been said to be good for skin problems and wounds, so many locals and travelers come specifically for skin care. According to one travel blog, the spring has been known since the Spanish period and is said to have been used to treat dysentery. Its medical benefits are not guaranteed, so treat this as background only. There is also a story that a 1903 medical journal reported dysentery patients being treated with this water, but today it is better to enjoy it as a relaxing experience rather than as a treatment.

As a tourist attraction it is small. Expect a couple of big pools, cottages, toilets and shower rooms, but no night lighting or lodging to speak of. In return, the entrance fee is only a few dozen pesos, and it fits well into a one- or two-hour stop combined with a Mt. Malindig climb or a tour of southern Marinduque. The information here was gathered from sources dated 2016 to 2026, so check the current operating status before you go.

In the same Malbog area there is a separate business called Marinduque Hot Spring Resort. It is run by a different operator and promotes day and night swimming, so to avoid mix-ups because of the similar names, tell your driver clearly which one you want.

blocks.title: Hot spring water from Mt. Malindig

children.text: The hot water is said to flow from the side of Mt. Malindig, the volcano in this area. Water keeps welling up from a round, stone-walled spring into the pool, and the overflow runs out into a small stream.
The water is a bluish white, and sulfur is mixed in so heavily that you can see it on the bottom and along the edges. It suits soaking and resting, whatever your swimming ability.

It has long been said to help with skin problems and wounds, so many people come on purpose. One visitor wrote of a prickly feeling on her face and foot. If your skin is sensitive, soak briefly first and see how your body reacts.
Sources list the entrance fee at about

You can rent a shaded cottage to leave your things and rest, and the toilets and shower rooms let you wash off after soaking. Some places reportedly also rent videoke equipment and floaters.

blocks.title: A natural follow-up to a Malindig climb

children.text: A sample itinerary on a travel blog schedules a Mt. Malindig hike first and then a rest at Malbog. Warm water suits legs that ache after the climb.

blocks.title: A neighborhood hot spring with locals

children.text: Villagers and families outnumber tourists, giving it a modest, unhurried feel. Weekday daytimes are quiet, and weekends and holidays are busier.

items.title: Mt. Malindig combo course
items.subtitle: Finish with a soak after the climb

children.text: Start the Mt. Malindig climb before dawn from the Sihi trailhead in Buenavista. Climb only in the dry season, and hiring a local guide is recommended.
After descending, rest at your lodging or in the village and refill water and snacks.
Take a tricycle to Malbog and loosen your muscles. The spring usually closes around 5 PM, so do not arrive late.
After showering, head into town, check the last jeepney time and go.
The climb depends heavily on your fitness and the weather, so leave some slack in your schedule. Mt. Malindig is classified as a potentially active volcano, so check the latest advisories.
One source says there are no scheduled commercial flights as of 2026, so most people combine a bus and a ferry. Marinduque Airport (MRQ) is used mainly for general aviation and charters.

items.title: From Buenavista town to the spring

children.text: In Buenavista Centro, take a tricycle and say "Malbog Hot Spring." One account puts it at about
3–5 minutes
from town.
A 2016 blogger wrote of a
round trip from a neighboring barangay, but fares may have risen since, so negotiate before you ride. Asking the driver to wait for you makes the return easier.
A separate business (Marinduque Hot Spring Resort) is in the same area, so state your destination clearly.
The water can be used year-round, but since you are soaking in warm water, the cool dry season is the most comfortable. One guide also names December–February as the best time.

In the rainy season, the unlit outdoor facilities are awkward to use when it rains, and a Mt. Malindig climb is recommended only in the dry season. Weekday mornings and late afternoons are quiet, while weekends and holidays are crowded.

Some sources mention rooms at the spring, but one account says they are not managed, and with no lighting it is hard to spend the night. Staying in Buenavista or Boac and visiting as a day trip is more realistic. Buenavista has a few farm-style resorts and family-run stays.

One guide says food is hard to find at the spring, so bringing water and snacks is wise. Shops in Buenavista town are said to sell Marinduque specialties such as bagoong (fermented shrimp paste), guyabano tea and bukayo sweets.

Marinduque does not see many travelers, so choices within Buenavista are limited. A convenient approach is to base your lodging and meals around Boac and visit the Buenavista spring and Mt. Malindig as a day trip. If you want to confirm hours and fees, contact the Buenavista municipal office or the spring's operator (including its Facebook page).
Bring a towel, a change of clothes, water, sunscreen, mosquito repellent and cash. ATMs are scarce, so prepare cash in advance.
The pool edges are rocky and can be slippery, so water shoes are a good idea.
Reviews say the sulfur smell can linger on your hair and body for up to 3 days. Tying up your hair and keeping your head out of the water, or wearing a rash guard, can reduce it.
Bring a sealable bag for wet swimwear and a spare towel for washing off the sulfur.
Keep the receipt when you pay the entrance fee. Locals advise making sure the fee goes to the municipal government.
Weekday mornings and late afternoons are quiet. Weekends and holidays are crowded.
Opening hours differ by source, from 6 AM or 8 AM to 5 PM. Check with the Buenavista local government (LGU) before you go.
Jewelry can tarnish in sulfur water, so it is better to take it off before getting in.

Reviews mention that the facilities are basic and some areas are dirty, so think of this as a local hot spring experience rather than expecting too much. Check the latest announcements for the operating status.
Reviews say there is no lighting, so night swimming and overnight stays are not possible. Leave before dark.
A review describes a chest-deep pool, so non-swimmers and children should use only shallow areas and be supervised.

Pregnant women, people with heart or respiratory conditions, and those with very sensitive skin should avoid long soaks and consult a doctor. Claims that it helps wounds or eczema are local folk belief.
Drinking the sulfur water is not recommended. Accounts say drinking therapy was used in the past, but do not try it today.
Jeepneys are said to stop around 4–5 PM, and ferries do not run under a typhoon signal.

The Sihi trailhead in Buenavista is the best known. Climb at dawn in the dry season and hiring a guide is recommended. It is often presented as a course followed by a soak at the spring.
